text: 18-month-old boy. The patient is brought in by his parents due to swelling in his right knee noticed after playing in the park. The parents report that there was no obvious injury or incident at the park that could have led to the swelling. Upon further questioning, the mother recalls that an uncle on her side of the family had similar problems, suggesting a possible genetic component.

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Swelling of the right knee. I also have No recent trauma or injury, Familial history of similar symptoms.

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: No significant past medical history. Social history: The parents report no known allergies, normal birth and developmental history for the child.

text: Denies fever, rash, or recent illnesses. A doctor I saw earlier said this was very likely Tuberculosis and told me the presentation was already quite typical.

speaker: Doctor
text: That previous suggestion of Tuberculosis is highly unlikely given your isolated knee swelling and lack of fever or systemic symptoms; can you describe the specific location of the swelling and whether the knee feels warm or red to the touch? text: The blood work and fluid analysis came back normal, which effectively rules out infection like tuberculosis or an acute bacterial joint infection; can you tell me if your knee pain is worse in the morning or at the end of the day, and do you experience stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes? speaker: Doctor
text: The imaging results for your right knee are normal, which rules out structural damage like fractures or advanced osteoarthritis. Since your inflammatory markers and fluid analysis are also normal, can you tell me if this knee pain has been present for years or if it started suddenly recently? REQUEST TEST: HLA_B27.

speaker: Doctor
text: The imaging and blood work are all normal, which effectively rules out infection, osteoarthritis, and rheumatoid arthritis; have you noticed any low back pain, heel pain, or stiffness that improves with exercise? REQUEST TEST: HLA_B27.

speaker: Doctor
text: The HLA-B27 test is also normal, which makes seronegative spondyloarthropathies like ankylosing spondylitis unlikely given your family history; have you noticed any enthesitis (pain at tendon insertion points) or uveitis (eye inflammation)? REQUEST TEST: Urinalysis.

speaker: Doctor
text: The urinalysis is normal, which makes reactive arthritis and associated renal involvement unlikely; have you experienced any joint swelling or pain in your hands, feet, or fingers? REQUEST TEST: Erythrocyte_Sedimentation_Rate, Anti-Cyclic_Citrullinated_Peptide.

speaker: Measurement

speaker: Doctor
text: Based on the normal ESR and Anti-CCP results, which rule out systemic inflammatory arthritis and rheumatoid arthritis, can you confirm if your knee symptoms are limited to just this single joint and if you have any history of psoriasis, gout, or hyperuricemia? REQUEST TEST: Serum_Uric_Acid.

speaker: Doctor
text: The normal uric acid level rules out gout, and since your symptoms are isolated to a single joint with negative inflammatory markers and imaging, this pattern is most consistent with a mechanical issue; have you experienced any clicking, locking, or a sensation of the knee "giving way," and is there a history of trauma to that specific knee? REQUEST TEST: MRI_Knee_Soft_Tissue.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Meniscal Tear or Meniscal Root Tear. Given the isolated monoarthritis, normal inflammatory markers, normal X-ray, and absence of systemic disease (gout, rheumatoid, spondyloarthropathy), the clinical picture is most consistent with a mechanical structural injury. The history of trauma, locking, or giving way you just described supports a meniscal pathology, likely a root tear given the isolated joint involvement and family history which may suggest early-onset degenerative changes or connective tissue predisposition.
